metadata.title: How Do You Know If You're Supervising Claude Enough?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether supervision of Claude is a flat personal habit (careful vs. not) or something that should scale with how much decision-making a given task hands over. Lands the carry-out that supervision is a measurable gap between usage level and verification time, invisible until it's logged.
metadata.source_note: Source is a CLI-explainer build of a log/classify/audit supervision-calibration tool (12-interaction demo, 50% score, 3 danger-corner interactions, revision loop, 2-week re-audit next step). Facts preserved: the log/classify/audit mechanism, the usage/supervision grid and danger-corner concept, the revision-adds-a-recommended-step loop, the run-a-week-then-re-audit next step. Dropped: the actual terminal commands, the Python code snippet, and the named classifier model (claude-3-5-haiku) -- general audience, no invented or stale product specifics. Register re-registered CLI/Teardown -> Plain; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (the source's own 12-interaction grid, literalized) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's CLI spine carried neither in the Plain sense. See QUESTION.md for full detail.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B05 (12-interaction usage/supervision grid, 3 danger-corner dots)

beats.narration_text: Someone wonders if they're careful enough with Claude. That's the wrong question — carefulness doesn't scale by task. What matters is whether your checking effort matches how much you're trusting it to decide. Liam explains.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Am I being careful enough with Claude?', hesitates on 'careful', corrects to 'calibrated', lands the real question

props.text:
Am I being
careful enough
with Claude?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('careful' -> 'calibrated') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that supervision is one habit — either you double-check things or you don't, and that habit follows you everywhere. But not every task hands Claude the same amount of trust: some are quick copy-paste edits, others are real decisions made mostly by the model. A flat habit can't track that difference. Only logging how much you actually verified, task by task, can — and the mismatch stays invisible until you do.

shot.new_visual_element: A single flat habit gauge, struck; a task-by-task log with levels against minutes checked, lit

production_viz.label: One flat habit, or logged task by task?
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a card labelled 'ONE FLAT HABIT' holding a single unchanging gauge/dial mark that never moves, no matter what's shown beside it. Right: a card labelled 'LOGGED, TASK BY TASK' with three entries: 'Level 1 -> 1 min', 'Level 2 -> 4 min', 'Level 3 -> 1 min' — the last line recolored terracotta as the mismatch. The left card dims and gets a terracotta strike; the right card stays lit.

beats.narration_text: The fix isn't trying harder to be careful — it's building something to log it. A small tool that does three things: log each interaction as it happens, classify how much decision-making you actually handed to Claude — a quick edit, an assisted task, or a real decision made mostly by the model — and once a week, audit for the gap: high-autonomy interactions that got almost no verification time.

shot.new_visual_element: A three-step flow: LOG, CLASSIFY, AUDIT

production_viz.label: Log, classify, audit
production_viz.mechanic: One card, three stacked steps connected by short arrows: '1. LOG the interaction', '2. CLASSIFY the level', '3. AUDIT the week for gaps'. Each step lights in sequence as the arrow reaches it; the third step's word 'GAPS' recolors terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Run it on a real week: twelve interactions, plotted on a grid — how much you relied on Claude across the bottom, how long you actually spent checking up the side. Most land near the diagonal, right where usage and verification match. Three sit in the danger corner: heavy reliance, almost no time spent checking at all.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- 12-dot usage/supervision grid, diagonal line, 3 red dots in the danger corner

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- twelve interactions, one grid
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A square grid: x-axis 'USAGE LEVEL' (low to high), y-axis 'VERIFICATION TIME' (low to high), a diagonal line from bottom-left to top-right. Twelve dots appear one at a time; nine land near the diagonal and recolor teal ('calibrated'), three land in the bottom-right corner (high usage, low verification) and recolor terracotta inside a dashed box labelled 'DANGER CORNER'. THIS EXACT GRID COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B05.

beats.narration_text: The three danger-corner interactions get named, not just counted. Each one gets a suggested next step, matched to what it actually was: a quick code check for a script that was never reviewed, a second opinion for a decision that leaned hard on Claude's judgment. The log turns from a report into a to-do list.

shot.new_visual_element: The 3 danger-corner dots, each tagged with a recommended-step label

production_viz.label: From report to to-do list
production_viz.mechanic: The three terracotta danger-corner dots from B03, now enlarged and arranged in a row. A small tag flies in beside each: 'code check', 'second opinion', 'code check'. A caption beneath reads 'REPORT -> TO-DO LIST', the arrow drawn once and held.

beats.narration_text: Run the audit again in two weeks, and the danger corner should empty out — that's real progress, the gap closing. But a rising score only proves you logged more checking time against those interactions; it doesn't prove the checking itself caught anything. And an interaction outside the danger corner isn't automatically fine — it just means this week's tool didn't flag it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- same grid, danger corner shrinks; splits into two both-directions cards

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- shrinking, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 GRID RETURNS, identical placement, but the danger corner now holds one dot instead of three (two have moved up toward the diagonal and recolored teal). It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'SCORE RISING' with an arrow to 'PROVES MORE LOGGED TIME' -- NOT to 'VERIFIED WELL' (struck through terracotta); right reads 'NOT FLAGGED' with an arrow to 'MISSED BY THIS PASS' -- NOT to 'AUTOMATICALLY FINE' (struck through terracotta).

beats.narration_text: Supervision isn't one habit you either have or don't — it's the gap between how much you're trusting Claude and how long you actually checked, and that gap stays invisible until you log it.

props.quote: Supervision isn't one habit you either have or don't — it's the gap between how much you're trusting Claude and how long you actually checked, and that gap stays invisible until you log it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Log ten interactions you've had with Claude this week, one sentence each. For each, note how much decision-making you handed over, and how many minutes you actually spent checking the result. Then look for the pattern: is your longest checking time going to the highest-trust interactions, or somewhere else? Liam, in for Bear.
